Ok, let's get some facts in here because the linked article is filled with speculation and that confuses people.

What you need to remember is that "pagefile" is not the same as "virtual memory".

Pagefile is virtual memory used by programs when the system runs out of ram.

At best you're adding in a 1% gain in some applications with a penalty of stability and 1% hit in other apps.

Also the page-file is a safety net but not just for programs when the system runs out of ram. As an example windows drivers are active in something called Page Pooled memory when the page pooled section runs out of memory it dumps the excess into the page file... and you don't have a page file you get system stability issues.

Also if you disable it you have to be mindful of how much RAM you're currently using with all your applications, games and background processes. I've burned through more than 16GB of ram with Chrome Alone (Yes, I'm a tab whore).

Disabling the pagefile became popular with the advent of SSDs where the first gen could be killed quickly by having your swapfiles on them. But technology advances. Add in TRIM support on SSDs and there is little reason to disable it. SSDs aren't hurt anymore by the swapping going on in an active page file. I have an SSD that I've been using in various computers as an OS drive with a page file for 5 years and it's remaining life is still estimated at more than 9 years.

Users frequently ask "how big should I make the pagefile?" There is no single answer to this question because it depends on the amount of installed RAM and on how much virtual memory that workload requires. If there is no other information available, the typical recommendation of 1.5 times the installed RAM is a good starting point. On server systems, you typically want to have sufficient RAM so that there is never a shortage and so that the pagefile is basically not used. On these systems, it may serve no useful purpose to maintain a really large pagefile. On the other hand, if disk space is plentiful, maintaining a large pagefile (for example, 1.5 times the installed RAM) does not cause a problem, and this also eliminates the need to worry over how large to make it.

"Virtual memory" is not the same as "pagefile". I mentioned that before but apparently you missed it.

Virtual memory is a wrapper for RAM and/or pagefile.

A virtual memory address may refer to RAM or pagefile.

When the memory being used by all the existing processes exceeds the available RAM, the operating system moves pages (4-KB pieces) of one or more virtual address spaces to the computer’s hard disk. This frees that RAM frame for other uses. In Windows systems, these “paged out” pages are stored in one or more files (Pagefile.sys files) in the root of a partition.

This is so that developers don't have to worry about memory management.

The above link is mentioned as "an expanded version" of the first article.

Here's another article from Microsoft that clearly states the difference between the two:

Virtual memory combines your computer’s RAM with temporary space on your hard disk. When RAM runs low, virtual memory moves data from RAM to a space called a paging file.

So if you disable pagefile the system will only use RAM.
